props.note: the chemical state (oxides) is not stated in this paper; supplied partially reduced

props.name: CO oxidation by catalyst improbable
props.statement: Oxidation of CO by the catalyst was improbable because the catalyst had been thoroughly reduced at 250 °C, above the 180 °C reaction temperature, with the reactant gas, and no degradation of catalytic activity to form carbon dioxide was observed.

props.name: CO2 formation grows with temperature
props.statement: In preliminary experiments at 160-230 °C, carbon dioxide formation was remarkable at higher temperatures while the reaction rate was too slow to observe below 180 °C; the temperature coefficient was therefore not measured and the temperature fixed at 180 °C.

props.name: deviation at low n (protium)
props.statement: Systematic deviation from the fitted equations is observed in the lower range of n for only the protium series (for all l-m-s combinations); calculated lines for Eqs. 8-10 overlap and the experimental points lie along them apart from this.

props.name: Eq. 8 abandoned
props.note: the 'established fact of pressure dependency' is the authors' premise from the literature, not a test of this source
props.statement: Estimated at elevated pressures, Eq. 8 gives a rate independent of pressure above 20 atm (Eqs. 9 and 10 do not); this contradicts the established pressure dependency of methanol synthesis, so Eq. 8 may be abandoned.

props.name: isotope effect in CO2 formation
props.statement: An isotope effect was found in the carbon dioxide formation at higher concentrations of carbon monoxide; the CO2 formed was near 20 mol% of the methanol in most runs, at most 30%.

props.name: no H/D isotope effect on methanol formation
props.statement: No deuterium isotope effect was observed in methanol synthesis: protium and deuterium points lie along the same line with no systematic deviation (Figs. 2 and 3), confirmed by changing the reactant gases in the order H-D-H-D-D.

props.name: no methane: path ii excluded
props.statement: Methane was absent from the circulating gas after several hours of reaction (gas chromatography), so the path 2CO + 2H2 = CO2 + CH4 was excluded.

props.name: rate equation not uniquely determined
props.statement: The range of experimental conditions was not wide enough to discriminate a single rate equation; the three equations reached all have adsorption terms of both hydrogen and carbon monoxide, as in the equation of Natta et al., with a different exponent s.

props.name: rM independent of space velocity
props.statement: No marked influence on rM was observed on changing the space velocity from 900 to 1800.

props.name: optimum n about 2
props.statement: The optimum methanol formation appears at an H2/CO (or D2/CO) ratio n of around 2 at 180 °C and 1 atm.

props.name: H2 = 2H(a); CO + 2H(a) -> CH2O(a); CH2O(a) + H(a) -> CH3O(a); CH3O(a) + H(a) -> CH3OH, step V rate-determining
props.statement: For Eq. 9 the reaction scheme may be H2 = 2H(a) (III), CO + 2H(a) -> CH2O(a) (IV), CH2O(a) + H(a) -> CH3O(a) (V), CH3O(a) + H(a) -> CH3OH (VI), with reaction V rate-determining.

props.name: CO adsorption rate-determining (view the authors reject)
props.statement: The absence of an isotope effect on methanol formation may give rise to the view that the adsorption of carbon monoxide is rate-determining.

props.name: CO2 formation on a site different from methanol formation
props.statement: The hydrogen isotope effect in CO2 formation, observed especially at higher CO concentrations where the methanol rate also deviates from the rate equation, may suggest that CO2 formation takes place on an active site different from that of methanol formation.

props.name: CO + H2 -> HCHO; HCHO + H2 -> CH3OH, reaction II rate-determining
props.statement: If methanol synthesis consists of CO + H2 -> HCHO (I) and HCHO + H2 -> CH3OH (II), Eq. 10 conforms to reaction II being rate-determining, because the partial pressure of HCHO is then K_I pH2 pCO.

props.name: rate-determining step involves hydrogen
props.statement: The rate equations suggest a rate-determining step in which hydrogen or a hydrogen-containing species is involved; reconciling this with the absent isotope effect requires further investigation.

props.name: methanol has no effect on rM under these conditions
props.statement: Since the variation in space velocity should give a different methanol vapor pressure in the catalyst bed, it seems that methanol has no effect on rM under the present conditions; the adsorption term of methanol may disappear because of the low conversion.
